words.def: Feeling thankful for something someone did for you.
words.ex: I'm so grateful for your help with the move.

words.def: Wanting to know or learn about something.
words.ex: The curious child asked why the sky is blue.

words.def: Able to wait calmly without getting upset.
words.ex: Be patient, the bus will come soon.
words.origin: From Middle English pacient, from Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of patior (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”).

words.def: Telling the truth and not trying to trick people.
words.ex: Thank you for giving me an honest answer.
words.origin: From Middle English honest, honeste (“honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor. For the verb, see Latin honestāre (“to clothe or adorn with honour”), and compare French honester.

words.def: Happy to give your time, money or help to others.
words.ex: My generous neighbour shared her lunch with me.
words.origin: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).

words.def: Ready to do something difficult or dangerous without showing fear.
words.ex: It was brave of you to speak in front of everyone.
words.origin: From Middle French brave, borrowed from Italian bravo, itself of uncertain origin (see there). Doublet of bravo.

words.def: Speaking and acting in a kind, respectful way.
words.ex: It is polite to say thank you when someone helps you.
words.origin: From Latin polītus (“polished”), past participle of poliō (“to polish, smooth”); see polish.

words.def: Worried or a little afraid about something that is going to happen.
words.ex: I always feel nervous before an exam.

words.def: Very pleased and happy.
words.ex: We were delighted to hear your good news.

words.def: Extremely tired.
words.ex: After the long walk home, I was exhausted.

words.def: Feeling sure that you can do something well.
words.ex: She felt confident after practising her speech.
words.origin: e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (“to trust fully, confide”).

words.def: Able to be trusted to do what you need or expect.
words.ex: He is a reliable friend who always shows up.

words.def: Happy and positive, and showing it.
words.ex: The cheerful waiter made our day better.
words.origin: From Middle English chereful, cherful, equivalent to cheer + -ful.

words.def: Worried and unable to relax.
words.ex: She was anxious about her mother's health.

words.def: Normal and not special in any way.
words.ex: It was an ordinary Tuesday until the phone rang.
words.origin: , Middle French ordinaire, and their source, Medieval Latin ordinarius, noun use of Latin ōrdinārius (“regular, orderly”), from ōrdō (“order”).

words.def: Known to you because you have seen or heard it before.
words.ex: Her face looked familiar, but I couldn't remember her name.

words.def: To succeed in doing something after working hard.
words.ex: You can achieve your goals if you keep going.

words.def: To make something better, or to become better.
words.ex: Reading every day will improve your vocabulary.

words.def: To give someone confidence or hope to do something.
words.ex: My teacher encouraged me to enter the competition.

words.def: To do something enjoyable because of a special day or event.
words.ex: We celebrated her birthday with a big dinner.

words.def: To say you are sorry for something you did.
words.ex: He apologised for arriving late.

words.def: To take something for a short time and give it back later.
words.ex: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
words.origin: From Middle English borwen, from Old English borgian (“to borrow, lend, pledge surety for”), from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną (“to pledge, take care of”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to take care”).

words.def: To make something clear and easy to understand.
words.ex: Can you explain how this machine works?
words.origin: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane.

words.def: To offer an idea for someone to think about.
words.ex: I suggest we leave early to avoid traffic.
words.origin: Coined based on Latin suggestus, perfect passive participle of suggerō (“bring up, bring under, lay beneath, furnish, supply, excite, advise, suggest”), from sub (“from below, under”) + gerō (“bear, carry”).

words.def: To like one thing more than another.
words.ex: I prefer tea to coffee in the morning.
words.origin: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō. Displaced native Old English foresettan and foreberan. Doublet of prelate.

words.def: To help someone remember something.
words.ex: Please remind me to call my mum tonight.
words.origin: From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind. Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate with the same sense. Displaced Old English myndgian.

words.def: To say that something is good and that someone should try it.
words.ex: Can you recommend a good book to read?
words.origin: From Middle English recommenden, from Old French recommender (compare French recommander), from Latin re- + commendāre (“to commend, commit; to recommend”), from con- + mandāre, from manus + dare.

words.def: To say that you are unhappy or annoyed about something.
words.ex: The customers complained about the cold food.
words.origin: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (“to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.

words.def: To say what someone or something is like.
words.ex: Describe your perfect weekend in three sentences.
words.origin: From Middle English descriven, from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībō (“to copy off, transcribe, sketch off, describe in painting or writing”), from dē (“off”) + scrībō (“write”); see scribe and shrive.

words.def: To find or learn something for the first time.
words.ex: We discovered a small café behind the market.
words.origin: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō.

words.def: To succeed in doing something difficult; or to be in charge of people or work.
words.ex: She managed to finish the report on time.

words.def: To act as if something is true when it is not.
words.ex: The children pretended to be pirates.

words.def: To suddenly understand or become aware of something.
words.ex: I realised I had left my keys at home.
words.origin: From real + -ise, possibly from French réaliser and Middle French réaliser (“to make real; to convert (something) into assets or cash”). See realize.

words.def: To pause before you do or say something because you are not sure.
words.ex: Don't hesitate to ask if you need help.

words.def: To be thankful for something; or to understand how good something is.
words.ex: I really appreciate your kind words.

words.def: To get better after an illness, injury or hard time.
words.ex: He recovered quickly after the operation.
words.origin: From Middle English recoveren, rekeveren, from Anglo-Norman recoverer and Old French recovrer, from Latin recuperāre, alternative form of reciperāre.

words.def: To speak very quietly, using your breath.
words.ex: She whispered the answer so the others wouldn't hear.
words.origin: From Middle English whisperen, from Old English hwisprian (“to mutter, murmur, whisper”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwisprōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweys-, *ḱwey- (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”).

words.def: To walk around slowly without a clear direction.
words.ex: We wandered through the old streets of the town.

words.def: To come together in one place, or to collect things.
words.ex: Families gathered in the square for the festival.
words.origin: From Middle English gaderen, from Old English gaderian (“to gather, assemble”), from Proto-West Germanic *gadurōn (“to bring together, unite, gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, assemble, keep”).

words.def: To save someone from danger.
words.ex: Firefighters rescued a cat from the roof.
words.origin: From Middle English rescouen, from Old French rescoure, rescurre, rescorre; from Latin prefix re- (“re-”) + excutere (“to shake or drive out”), from ex (“out”) + quatiō (“to shake”).

words.def: To have earned something because of what you did.
words.ex: You worked hard and you deserve a rest.
words.origin: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- + serviō.

words.def: To make air, water or land dirty and harmful.
words.ex: Factories should not pollute the river.
words.origin: From Middle English polluten, borrowed from Latin pollūtum, from pollūtus (“no longer virgin", "unchaste”), perfect passive participle of polluō (“soil", "defile", "dishonor”).

words.def: A chance to do something good or useful.
words.ex: This job is a great opportunity to learn.
words.origin: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.

words.def: Knowledge or skill you get from doing something; or something that happens to you.
words.ex: Travelling alone was an amazing experience.
words.origin: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past participle of *periri (“to go through”); see expert and peril.

words.def: An opinion about what someone should do.
words.ex: My grandmother gave me good advice about saving money.

words.def: The way you think and feel about something.
words.ex: A positive attitude makes hard work easier.
words.origin: From French attitude, from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) and actitūdō (“acting, posture”), from Latin aptō and actitō.

words.def: Something you do often, usually without thinking.
words.ex: Reading before bed is a good habit.
words.origin: From Middle English habit, from Latin habitus (“condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”). Distantly related to gift.

words.def: Something difficult that tests your ability.
words.ex: Learning a new language is a fun challenge.

words.def: A trip from one place to another, usually a long one.
words.ex: The journey from Lagos to Abuja took all day.

words.def: Something you remember from the past; or the ability to remember.
words.ex: My favourite memory is swimming at the beach with my dad.
words.origin: , from Latin memoria (“the faculty of remembering, remembrance, memory, a historical account”), from memor (“mindful, remembering”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (to remember), related to Ancient Greek μνήμη (“memory”) μέρμερος (“anxious”), μέριμνα (“care, thought”), Old English ġemimor (“mindful, remembering”).

words.def: A person who lives next to you or near you.
words.ex: Our neighbour waters our plants when we travel.

words.def: A good feeling when something bad or worrying stops.
words.ex: It was a relief to find my lost phone.
words.origin: From Old French relief (“assistance”), from Old French relever (“to relieve”), from Latin relevare (“to raise up, make light”). See also relieve.

words.def: The ability to wait or keep trying without getting angry.
words.ex: Teaching small children takes a lot of patience.

words.def: An angry talk between people who disagree; or reasons for an opinion.
words.ex: They had an argument about who should drive.

words.def: Something that is wrong or done wrongly.
words.ex: Everyone makes mistakes when learning.

words.def: The reason why something is done or made.
words.ex: What is the purpose of this meeting?

words.def: The ability to do something well, usually after practice.
words.ex: Cooking is a useful skill to learn.
words.origin: From Middle English skill, skille (also schil, schile), from Old Norse skil (“a distinction, discernment, knowledge”), from Proto-Germanic *skilją (“separation, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”).

words.def: How hot or cold something is.
words.ex: The temperature dropped quickly at night.
words.origin: Latin temperātūra (cf. also French température), from the past participle stem of tempero (“to temper”).

words.def: The air, water and land where people, animals and plants live.
words.ex: We should protect the environment for future generations.

words.def: A group of people who live in the same area or share something.
words.ex: The whole community helped clean the park.

words.def: A choice you make after thinking.
words.ex: Moving abroad was a big decision.
words.origin: Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

words.def: An unexpected event or feeling.
words.ex: The party was a complete surprise.
words.origin: From Middle English surprise, borrowed from Middle French surprise (“an overtake”), nominal use of the past participle of Old French sorprendre (“to overtake”), from sor- (“over”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin super- + Latin prendere, contracted from prehendere (“to grasp, seize”).

words.def: Luck, or a very large amount of money.
words.ex: By good fortune, the rain stopped just before the wedding.
words.origin: From Middle English fortune, from Old French fortune, from Latin fortuna (“fate, luck”). The plural form fortunae meant “possessions”, which also gave fortune the meaning of “riches”.

words.def: Very old; from a long time ago.
words.ex: We visited the ancient walls of Benin City.

words.def: Uncomfortable or embarrassing; or difficult to use.
words.ex: There was an awkward silence after his joke.

words.def: Full of people.
words.ex: The market is always crowded on Saturdays.

words.def: Tasting very good.
words.ex: The jollof rice was delicious.

words.def: Extremely big.
words.ex: An enormous tree stood in the middle of the field.
words.origin: From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- + norma (“rule, norm”) + -ous.

words.def: Easily broken or damaged.
words.ex: Be careful, the glass vase is fragile.
words.origin: Middle French fragile, from Latin fragilis, formed on frag-, the root of frangere (“to break”). Cognate with fraction, fracture and Doublet of frail.

words.def: Kind and calm; not rough or strong.
words.ex: He was gentle with the baby.

words.def: Not thinking you are better than other people.
words.ex: Despite her success, she stayed humble.
words.origin: From Middle English humble, from Old French humble, umble, humle, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμηλός (“on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”).

words.def: Always supporting a person or group.
words.ex: The dog was loyal to its owner for years.

words.def: Quiet and calm, without trouble.
words.ex: The village is peaceful in the early morning.

words.def: Very valuable or very important to you.
words.ex: Time with family is precious.

words.def: Not common; not happening often.
words.ex: It's rare to see snow here.
words.origin: From Middle English rare, from Old French rare, rere (“rare, uncommon”), from Latin rārus (“loose, spaced apart, thin, infrequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“friable, thin”).

words.def: Showing good judgement.
words.ex: Wearing a helmet is a sensible choice.
words.origin: From Latin sēnsibilis (“perceptible by the senses, having feeling, sensible”), from sentiō (“to feel, perceive”).

words.def: Making no sound at all.
words.ex: The classroom went silent when the head teacher walked in.

words.def: Refusing to change your mind.
words.ex: My brother is too stubborn to admit he's wrong.

words.def: Thinking about other people's feelings; or thinking deeply.
words.ex: It was thoughtful of you to bring flowers.
words.origin: From Middle English thoȝtful, thohtful, equivalent to thought + -ful. Compare Dutch gedachtenvol, Swedish tankfull.

words.def: Neat and in order.
words.ex: Please keep your room tidy.

words.def: Needing to be dealt with immediately.
words.ex: I have an urgent message for the manager.

words.def: Very clear, bright or detailed.
words.ex: I had a vivid dream about flying.

words.def: Having a lot of money.
words.ex: A wealthy businessman paid for the new library.
words.origin: From Middle English welthy, welþi, equivalent to wealth + -y. Cognate with Middle Dutch weldech, weeldech (“magnificent, luscious, lavish”).

words.def: Extremely angry.
words.ex: She was furious when someone scratched her car.
words.origin: From Middle English furious, from Old French furieus, from Latin furiōsus. Displaced native Old English hātheort.

words.def: Confused because you cannot understand something.
words.ex: He looked puzzled by the question.

words.def: Pleased about something you or someone close to you did.
words.ex: My parents were proud when I graduated.
words.origin: From Middle English proud, prout, prut, from Old English prūd, prūt (“proud, arrogant, haughty”) (compare Old English prȳtung (“pride”); prȳde, prȳte (“pride”), see also Old English deal), probably from Old French prod, prut (“brave, gallant”) (modern French preux), from Late Latin prōde (“useful”), derived from Latin prōdesse (“to be of value”); however, the Old English umlaut derivatives prȳte, prȳtian, etc.

words.def: Wanting very much to do or have something.
words.ex: The students were eager to start the trip.

words.def: Relaxed and not worried or excited.
words.ex: Stay calm and read the instructions again.

words.def: Lasting a short time; using few words.
words.ex: She gave a brief speech to thank everyone.
words.origin: From Middle English breef, breve, bref, from Old French brief, bref, from Latin brevis (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short, brief”).

words.def: Completely necessary; extremely important.
words.ex: Water is essential for life.

words.def: Easy to see or understand.
words.ex: It was obvious that he was tired.
words.origin: 16th century, from la:obvius + -ous, from ob- (“before”) + via (“way”).

words.def: Right or acceptable for a particular purpose.
words.ex: This film is not suitable for young children.

words.def: Able to be used or got; free to talk or meet.
words.ex: Are you available for a call this afternoon?
words.origin: From Middle English available, avayllable, avayleable, equivalent of avail + -able.

words.def: Correct and exact, without mistakes.
words.ex: The weather forecast was accurate today.
words.origin: Compare English cure.

words.def: Easy to use or suitable for your plans.
words.ex: Is Friday a convenient time to meet?
words.origin: From Middle English convenient, from Latin conveniēns (“fit, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō, convinīre (“to come together, suit”); see convene and compare covenant.

words.def: Working well without wasting time or energy.
words.ex: The new system is much more efficient.
words.origin: 1398, “making,” from Old French, from Latin efficientem, nominative efficiēns, participle of efficere (“work out, accomplish”) (see effect).

words.def: Able to change easily; able to bend.
words.ex: My job has flexible working hours.
words.origin: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + -ible.

words.def: Not needing help or control from others.
words.ex: She became independent after moving to the city.
words.origin: From Middle English independent, equivalent to in- + dependent. Compare French indépendant.

words.def: Kind and wanting to help other people.
words.ex: The benevolent doctor treated poor patients for free.
words.origin: From Old French benevolent, borrowed from Latin benevolēns ("benevolent"). Displaced native Old English welwillende (literally well-wishing).

words.def: Able to recover quickly after something difficult.
words.ex: Children are often more resilient than we think.

words.def: Working hard and carefully.
words.ex: A diligent student reviews her notes every day.
words.origin: From Middle English diligent, from Old French diligent, from Latin dīligēns (“careful, attentive, diligent”), present participle of dīligō (“to love, esteem much”), from dī-, dis- (“apart”) + legō (“to choose”); see elect and select.

words.def: Able to speak or write clearly and persuasively.
words.ex: Her eloquent speech moved the whole audience.
words.origin: From Old French eloquent, from Latin eloquens (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of eloquor (“to speak out”), from e (“out”) + loquor (“to speak”).

words.def: Having more than one possible meaning, so not clear.
words.ex: The instructions were ambiguous, so we asked again.

words.def: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
words.ex: Change is inevitable, so we may as well prepare.
words.origin: From Middle French inevitable, from Latin inēvītābilis (“unavoidable”), from in- + ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- (“out”) + vītāre (“to shun”).

words.def: Seeming reasonable or likely to be true.
words.ex: His excuse was plausible, but I still had doubts.
words.origin: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

words.def: Not wanting to do something.
words.ex: She was reluctant to lend him more money.

words.def: Easily hurt, harmed or attacked.
words.ex: Old people are more vulnerable to the cold.
words.origin: From Late Latin vulnerābilis (“injurious, wounding”), from Latin vulnerō (“to wound”).

words.def: Happening naturally, without planning.
words.ex: We made a spontaneous trip to the beach.

words.def: Very careful about every small detail.
words.ex: He keeps meticulous notes in every meeting.
words.origin: Latin meticulōsus (“full of fear, timid, fearful, terrible, frightful”), from metus (“fear”) and -culōsus, extracted from perīculōsus (“perilous”).

words.def: Honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
words.ex: Thank you for your candid feedback on my work.

words.def: Careful not to spend more money than needed.
words.ex: Being frugal helped them save for a house.
words.origin: From Middle French, from Latin frugalis (“virtuous, thrifty”). Displaced native Old English spærhende.

words.def: Boring because it is long, slow or repetitive.
words.ex: Filling in the forms was tedious but necessary.
words.origin: English tedium + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

words.def: Able to do many different things well, or to be used in many ways.
words.ex: A versatile player can play in any position.
words.origin: From Latin versātilis (“turning easily”), from versātus, past participle of versō (“to turn, change”), frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

words.def: No longer used because something newer exists.
words.ex: Fax machines are almost obsolete.
words.origin: Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of obsolēscere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see obsolesce.

words.def: Real and true, not fake or pretended.
words.ex: Her smile was warm and genuine.

words.def: Important and well known; or easy to see.
words.ex: She is a prominent lawyer in Lagos.
words.origin: From obsolete French prominent (compare proéminent), from Latin prōminēns, present active participle of prōmineō (“jut out, to project”), from prō (“before, forward”) + mineō (in compounds, “jut, project”).

words.def: Large in amount, size or importance.
words.ex: The company made a substantial profit this year.
words.origin: From Middle English substancial, substantiall, from Old French substanciel, substantiel and its etymon Latin substantiālis.

words.def: Good enough or enough in amount.
words.ex: Make sure you get adequate sleep before the exam.

words.def: Clear and logical, with parts that fit together.
words.ex: Write a coherent argument with a clear conclusion.

words.def: Saying a lot in few words.
words.ex: Keep your email concise and polite.
words.origin: From Latin concīsus (“cut short”), from concīdere (“cut to pieces”), from caedēre (“to cut, to strike down”).

words.def: Possible and practical to do.
words.ex: Is it feasible to finish the project by Friday?
words.origin: From Anglo-Norman fesable, from Latin facere, Old French fesable, faisable (“doable”), from fere, faire (“to do”) + -able.

words.def: Unfriendly and ready to fight or argue.
words.ex: The crowd became hostile when the match was cancelled.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French hostile, from Latin hostīlis, from hostis (“enemy”). Displaced Old English fēondlīċ.

words.def: Being a basic, natural part of something.
words.ex: There are risks inherent in any new business.

words.def: Feeling happy and a little sad when you think about the past.
words.ex: Old photos always make me nostalgic.

words.def: Expecting good things to happen.
words.ex: We are optimistic about the results.

words.def: Expecting bad things to happen.
words.ex: He is pessimistic about the economy.

words.def: Continuing to try, even when it is difficult; or lasting a long time.
words.ex: Her persistent effort finally paid off.

words.def: Very great or deep; showing deep understanding.
words.ex: The book had a profound effect on me.
words.origin: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).

words.def: Stiff and hard to bend; or not willing to change.
words.ex: The school has rigid rules about uniforms.

words.def: Doubting that something is true or useful.
words.ex: I'm sceptical about diets that promise quick results.

words.def: Not obvious; small but important.
words.ex: There's a subtle difference between the two colours.

words.def: Small and unimportant.
words.ex: Don't argue about trivial things.

words.def: Not clear or detailed.
words.ex: He gave a vague answer about his plans.
words.origin: From Middle French vague, from Latin vagus (“uncertain, vague”).

words.def: Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
words.ex: The region has abundant natural resources.
words.origin: First attested about 1380. From Middle English abundaunt, habundaunt, aboundant, from Anglo-Norman abundant, from Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“to overflow, to abound”).

words.def: Real and true to its origin; not a copy.
words.ex: This restaurant serves authentic Yoruba dishes.
words.origin: From Middle English authentik, from Old French autentique, from Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (“authentic, genuine”), from Ancient Greek αὐθέντης (“autonomous actor, perpetrator, murderer, absolute ruler”).

words.def: Extremely important; deciding what happens next.
words.ex: The next few days are crucial for the project.
words.origin: 1706, from French crucial, a medical term for ligaments of the knee (which cross each other), from Latin crux, crucis (“cross”) (English crux), from the Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”).

words.def: Including many different types of people or things.
words.ex: Lagos is a diverse and busy city.

words.def: Clear and easy to see or understand.
words.ex: It was evident that she had practised a lot.
words.origin: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”).

words.def: Very interested and eager.
words.ex: He is keen to learn how to code.
words.origin: From Middle English kene (“bold, brave, sharp”), from Old English cēne (“keen, fierce, bold, brave, warlike, powerful; learned, clever, wise”), from Proto-Germanic *kōniz (“knowledgeable, skilful, experienced, clever, capable”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).

words.def: Ordinary and not interesting.
words.ex: Even mundane tasks can be fun with good music.
words.origin: From Middle English mondeyne, from Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”). Compare Danish mondæn.

words.def: Too ready to believe things because of little experience.
words.ex: It was naive to think the job would be easy.
words.origin: , feminine form of naïf, from Latin nātīvus (“native, natural”). Doublet of native.

words.def: Famous for something bad.
words.ex: The road is notorious for traffic jams.

words.def: Full of happiness or love, so you seem to shine; or shining brightly.
words.ex: The bride looked radiant on her wedding day.
words.origin: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).

words.def: Honest and meaning what you say.
words.ex: Please accept my sincere apologies.

words.def: Calm, quiet and peaceful.
words.ex: The lake was tranquil in the early morning.
words.origin: Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).

words.def: To expect something and often prepare for it.
words.ex: We anticipate a large crowd at the concert.

words.def: To make something clearer or easier to understand.
words.ex: Could you clarify what you mean by "soon"?
words.origin: From Middle English clarifien, from Old French clarifiier, from Latin clārificō, clārificāre; clārus (“clear”) + faciō, facere (“make”). Semantically clear + -ify.

words.def: To work together with others on something.
words.ex: Two schools collaborated on the science project.
words.origin: Back-formation from collaborator, from French collaborateur, or else modeled on French collaborer or directly from Late Latin collabōrātus, past participle of collabōrāre.

words.def: To agree by each side accepting less than they wanted.
words.ex: We compromised and ate at a place we both liked.
words.origin: From Middle French compromis, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin compromissum (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop.

words.def: To think carefully about something for a long time.
words.ex: She contemplated moving abroad for work.

words.def: To become worse.
words.ex: His health deteriorated during the winter.

words.def: To show that something is especially important.
words.ex: The coach emphasised the need for teamwork.

words.def: To improve the quality or value of something.
words.ex: Good lighting can enhance a photo.

words.def: To judge how good, useful or successful something is.
words.ex: Teachers evaluate students in different ways.
words.origin: Back-formation from evaluation.

words.def: To change often between higher and lower levels.
words.ex: Prices fluctuate depending on the season.

words.def: To explain something by giving examples; or to add pictures to a book.
words.ex: Let me illustrate my point with a story.
words.origin: Back-formation from illustration.

words.def: To give a good reason for something.
words.ex: How can you justify spending so much on shoes?
words.origin: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.

words.def: To talk with others to reach an agreement.
words.ex: They negotiated a better price for the car.

words.def: To succeed in dealing with a problem or difficulty.
words.ex: She overcame her fear of flying.

words.def: To make someone agree to do or believe something.
words.ex: He persuaded his parents to let him go to the party.
words.origin: From Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”). Cognate to for, sweet.

words.def: To move an event to a later time.
words.ex: The match was postponed because of the rain.
words.origin: From Latin postpōnō (“to put after; to postpone”) from post (“after”) + pōnō (“to put; to place”), compare forestall.

words.def: To decide which things are most important and do them first.
words.ex: Learn to prioritise your tasks each morning.

words.def: To make two people friends again after an argument; or to make two ideas fit together.
words.ex: The sisters reconciled after years apart.

words.def: To look at or examine something very carefully.
words.ex: The manager scrutinised every line of the budget.

words.def: To make something or someone weaker, often gradually.
words.ex: Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.

words.def: To publicly support an idea or plan.
words.ex: She advocates free education for all children.

words.def: To make pain or a problem less severe.
words.ex: This medicine will alleviate the headache.

words.def: A situation where you must make a difficult choice.
words.ex: I faced a dilemma: work late or miss my sister's play.

words.def: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
words.ex: Good nurses show empathy to their patients.

words.def: Being honest and having strong moral principles.
words.ex: We need a leader with integrity.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French intégrité, from Latin integritās (“soundness, integrity”), from integer. Doublet of entirety.

words.def: A particular way of thinking about something.
words.ex: Travel gives you a new perspective on life.
words.origin: From Middle English perspective, perspectif, attested since 1381, from Old French or Middle French, from the first word of the Medieval Latin perspectiva ars (“science of optics”), the feminine of Latin perspectivus (“of sight, optical”), from perspectus, the past participle of perspicere (“to inspect, look through”), itself from per- (“through”) + specere (“to look at”); the noun sense was influenced or mediated by Italian prospettiva, from prospetto (“prospect”).

words.def: A result of something, often a bad one.
words.ex: Every choice has consequences.
words.origin: From Middle English consequence, from Old French consequence, from Latin consequentia. While analysable as con- + sequence, its adjective form has a different origin.

words.def: The ability to act without being told; or a new plan.
words.ex: She took the initiative and fixed the problem herself.

words.def: Something that encourages you to do something.
words.ex: The bonus is an incentive to work harder.

words.def: A very small difference in meaning, feeling or colour.
words.ex: Translators must understand every nuance of a text.
words.origin: French nuance. Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs.

words.def: Something that blocks your way or makes progress difficult.
words.ex: Lack of money was the biggest obstacle.
words.origin: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.

words.def: A situation or statement that seems impossible because it has two opposite facts.
words.ex: It's a paradox that the more you learn, the less you feel you know.
words.origin: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (“unexpected, strange”).

words.def: Something that happens or exists, especially something unusual.
words.ex: Northern lights are a natural phenomenon.

words.def: An action taken to prevent something bad from happening.
words.ex: Take an umbrella as a precaution.
words.origin: From French précaution, Latin praecautio, from praecavere, praecautum (“to guard against beforehand”); prae (“before”) + cavere (“be on one's guard”).

words.def: Not wanting to do something.
words.ex: He agreed, but with obvious reluctance.
words.origin: From Latin relū̆ctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”) + -ance, from re- (“back”) + luctor (“to struggle”).

words.def: A lack of something that is needed.
words.ex: The scarcity of water is a serious problem.

words.def: Something that delays or stops progress.
words.ex: The injury was a setback, but she recovered.

words.def: The level at which something starts to happen; or the floor at a doorway.
words.ex: She paused at the threshold before entering.
words.origin: From Middle English threschwolde, threscholde, from Old English þresċold, þerxold, þrexwold (“doorsill, entryway”), from Proto-Germanic *þreskudlaz, *þreskūþlijaz, *þreskwaþluz, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną, *þreskwaną (“to thresh, (originally) to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn”).

words.def: The ability to do or be used for many different things.
words.ex: The chef is known for his versatility.

words.def: Giving a lot of time and effort to something you believe in.
words.ex: Her dedication to her patients is inspiring.
words.origin: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English dedicacioun, from Old French dedicacion (“consecration of a church or chapel”), from Latin dēdicātiō, equivalent to dēdicātus+-iōn.

words.def: A strong feeling of excitement and interest.
words.ex: The class showed great enthusiasm for the trip.
words.origin: First attested from 1603, from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός, from ἐν (“in”) + θεός (“god”) + οὐσία (“essence”).

words.def: An idea that has not yet been proved, which you test.
words.ex: Test your hypothesis with a simple experiment.
words.origin: Recorded since 1596, from Middle French hypothese, from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (“base, basis of an argument, supposition”), itself from ὑποτίθημι (“to set before, suggest”), from ὑπό (“below”) + τίθημι (“to put, place”).

words.def: A clear, deep understanding of something.
words.ex: The interview gave us insight into her life.

words.def: Something left behind by a person or event for the future.
words.ex: His legacy is the school he built.
words.origin: From Middle English legacie, from Old French legacie and Medieval Latin lēgātia, from Latin lēgātum. Compare legatee.

words.def: An important event or stage in a process.
words.ex: Finishing the first draft was a big milestone.

words.def: The force that keeps something moving or developing.
words.ex: The campaign gained momentum after the debate.

words.def: A set of actions always done in the same way.
words.ex: Morning tea is my favourite ritual.
words.origin: From Latin rītuālis, from rītus + -ālis. Displaced native Old English ġewuna and wuna.

words.def: Luck in finding good things by chance.
words.ex: Meeting my best friend on a delayed train was pure serendipity.
words.origin: From Serendip + -ity. Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 based on the Persian story of the Three Princes of Serendip, who (Walpole wrote to a friend) were “always making discoveries, by accidents and sagacity, of things which they were not in quest of”.

words.def: Lasting a very short time.
words.ex: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.
words.origin: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος, the more common form of ἐφημέριος (“of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (“on”) + ἡμέρα (“day”).

words.def: Seeming to be everywhere at the same time.
words.ex: Mobile phones are now ubiquitous.
words.origin: From ubiquity + -ous, from Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque (“everywhere”), from ubī̆ (“where”) + -que (“each, ever”). Compare ubiety.

words.def: The skill of speaking or writing well and persuasively.
words.ex: The poet's eloquence brought tears to our eyes.

words.def: Being the most typical example of something.
words.ex: Jollof rice is the quintessential party food.

words.def: Happening by chance, usually in a lucky way.
words.ex: Our fortuitous meeting led to a great job offer.

words.def: Generous and kind, especially towards a rival or someone weaker.
words.ex: The champion was magnanimous in victory.
words.origin: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”). Displaced native Old English miċelmōd.

words.def: Done quickly and without real care or interest.
words.ex: He gave a perfunctory nod and kept reading.
words.origin: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

words.def: Dealing with problems in a sensible, practical way.
words.ex: We need a pragmatic solution, not a perfect one.
words.origin: ”), from πράσσω (“to do”) (whence English practical).

words.def: Showing off wealth or importance to impress people.
words.ex: They threw an ostentatious party with gold plates.
words.origin: Originated 1590; from la:ostentātus + -ious.

words.def: Using very few words.
words.ex: His laconic reply was simply "No."

words.def: Clear and easy to understand; or able to think clearly.
words.ex: She gave a lucid explanation of a complex topic.

words.def: Extreme care about every small detail.
words.ex: Her meticulousness made the report flawless.

words.def: A loud, unpleasant mix of sounds.
words.ex: The market was a cacophony of horns and voices.

words.def: A gentle word used instead of one that might upset or offend.
words.ex: "Passed away" is a euphemism for "died".
words.origin: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός, from εὐφημίζω, from εὔφημος (“uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (“well”) + φήμη (“a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (“to speak, say”).

words.def: Placing two different things side by side to compare them.
words.ex: The juxtaposition of old and new buildings is striking.
words.origin: French juxtaposition, from Latin iuxtā (“near”) (from Latin iungō (“to join”)) + French position (“position”) (from Latin pōnō (“to place”)).

words.def: Calmness, especially in a difficult situation.
words.ex: She accepted the bad news with equanimity.

words.def: Quick and cheerful readiness to do something.
words.ex: He accepted the invitation with alacrity.
words.origin: Mid-15th century; from Middle English alacrite, from Latin alacritās, from alacer (“brisk”) + -itās (“-ity”).

words.def: Wise and showing good judgement.
words.ex: The sagacious elder settled the dispute fairly.
words.origin: Coined between 1600 and 1610. Borrowed from Latin sagāx, + -acious.

words.def: Enjoying the company of other people.
words.ex: Gregarious people often love big parties.
words.origin: ; Latin gregārius, see -ious.

words.def: Unusual and specific to one person.
words.ex: He has an idiosyncratic way of tying his shoes.

words.def: Perfect, with no faults at all.
words.ex: Her manners were impeccable.
words.origin: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

words.def: Never seeming to get tired.
words.ex: The indefatigable volunteers worked through the night.
words.origin: From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).

words.def: Impossible to stop or prevent.
words.ex: The inexorable rise of prices worried everyone.

words.def: Spreading or developing slowly and secretly in a harmful way.
words.ex: Stress can have an insidious effect on health.
words.origin: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

words.def: Talking a lot.
words.ex: Our loquacious taxi driver told us his whole life story.
words.origin: From loquāx + -ous or from loquacity + -ous, ultimately from Latin loquor + -acious.

words.def: Sweet and smooth to listen to.
words.ex: She has a mellifluous singing voice.
words.origin: From Middle English mellifluous,mellyfluous, from Latin mellifluus (“flowing like honey”) + -ous, from mel (“honey”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare superfluous and fluid, from same root, and with dulcet (“sweet speech”), alternative Latinate term with a similar meaning.

words.def: Calm and seeming not to care or worry.
words.ex: He gave a nonchalant shrug when he won.
words.origin: French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- + chaloir, from Latin non + calēre.

words.def: To make something deliberately unclear or confusing.
words.ex: The report used jargon to obfuscate the problem.

words.def: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually.
words.ex: Rumours can have a pernicious effect on a team.
words.origin: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

words.def: Refusing to obey or cooperate.
words.ex: The recalcitrant goat would not leave the road.

words.def: Hopeful and positive, especially in a difficult situation.
words.ex: Investors remain sanguine about the market.

words.def: More than is needed; unnecessary.
words.ex: Cut any superfluous words from your essay.
words.origin: From Middle English superfluous, from Latin superfluus (“superfluous”) + -ous, from superfluō (“overflow”), from super (“above, more than, over”) + fluō (“flow”).

words.def: Holding firmly to something; not giving up.
words.ex: A tenacious reporter finally got the story.
words.origin: From Latin tenāx (“holding fast, clinging”), from tenēre (“to hold”), + -ious.

words.def: Respected because of age, wisdom or long history.
words.ex: The venerable professor taught for fifty years.
words.origin: From Middle French vénérable, from Old French, from Latin venerabilis.

words.def: Showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause.
words.ex: Zealous fans waited outside the stadium all night.

words.def: To accept or agree to something, often without saying so strongly.
words.ex: She acquiesced to her parents' wishes.
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French acquiescer, from Latin acquiescō; ad + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).

words.def: To make a bad situation better.
words.ex: New laws helped to ameliorate living conditions.

words.def: To stop resisting and agree to something.
words.ex: After hours of talks, the company capitulated.

words.def: To find a way around a rule or problem.
words.ex: They tried to circumvent the security checks.

words.def: To support a statement with evidence.
words.ex: Witnesses corroborated her version of events.

words.def: To spread information widely.
words.ex: The ministry disseminated health advice across the country.

words.def: To make a problem worse.
words.ex: Shouting will only exacerbate the situation.

words.def: To use known facts to guess about the future or something unknown.
words.ex: We can extrapolate future sales from this year's data.

words.def: To shock or excite people into taking action.
words.ex: The speech galvanised the students into action.

words.def: To make something less harmful or serious.
words.ex: Trees help mitigate the effects of flooding.

words.def: To increase quickly in number.
words.ex: Fast food shops have proliferated in the city.
words.origin: Back-formation from proliferation.

words.def: To refuse to accept or be associated with something.
words.ex: The leader repudiated the violent protests.

words.def: To provide evidence that something is true.
words.ex: Can you substantiate your claim with data?
words.origin: From Medieval Latin substantiatus (“given substance”), from the verb substantiare, first used 1657.

words.def: To prove that someone or something was right or not to blame.
words.ex: The results vindicated her decision.
words.origin: Latin vindicātus, perfect passive participle of vindicō (“lay legal claim to something; set free; protect, avenge, punish”), from vim, accusative singular of vīs (“force, power”), + dīcō (“say; declare, state”).

words.def: Having mixed feelings about something.
words.ex: I'm ambivalent about moving to a new city.
words.origin: Back-formation from ambivalence, from German Ambivalenz, from Latin ambi- (“in two ways”) + valeō (“be strong”); equivalent to ambi + valent.

words.def: Something that is different from what is normal or expected.
words.ex: The low score was an anomaly in her excellent record.

words.def: A division into two very different or opposite things.
words.ex: There is a dichotomy between what he says and what he does.
words.origin: From Ancient Greek διχοτομία (“dichotomy”).

words.def: Things that are useful or enjoyed for only a short time, such as tickets and posters.
words.ex: The museum collects concert ephemera.
words.origin: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερᾰ, neuter plural form of ἐφήμερος.

words.def: Too much pride and confidence, which often leads to failure.
words.ex: His hubris made him ignore every warning.
words.origin: Ancient Greek ὕβρις (“pride, insolence, outrage”).

words.def: A typical model or pattern; a set of ideas that explain something.
words.ex: The internet created a new paradigm for business.

words.def: A practical way of dealing with problems.
words.ex: Her pragmatism helped the team reach a decision.
words.origin: From Ancient Greek stem of πρᾶγμα (“act”) + -ism.

words.def: A state of not knowing what to do in a difficult situation.
words.ex: I'm in a quandary about which job to accept.

words.def: A pleasant state of daydreaming.
words.ex: The phone rang and broke her reverie.

words.def: Pleasure felt at someone else's bad luck.
words.ex: He felt a little schadenfreude when his rival lost.

words.def: Comfort in a time of sadness or worry.
words.ex: She found solace in music after the loss.
words.origin: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).

words.def: The quality of not giving up easily.
words.ex: Her tenacity helped her pass the exam on the third try.

words.def: The quality of seeming real or true.
words.ex: The film's verisimilitude made it feel like a documentary.
words.origin: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).

words.def: The general mood or ideas of a particular time.
words.ex: The song captured the zeitgeist of the 1990s.
words.origin: German Zeitgeist.

words.def: Kind and gentle; or not harmful.
words.ex: The doctor said the lump was benign.
words.origin: From Middle English benigne, benygne, from Old French benigne, from Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bene (“well”) + genus (“origin, kind”).

words.def: The quality of being open and honest.
words.ex: I appreciated the candour of her feedback.

words.def: Clear, logical and convincing.
words.ex: She presented a cogent case for the new policy.
words.origin: From French cogent, from Latin cōgēns, present active participle of cōgō (“drive together, compel”), from cō + agō (“drive”).

words.def: A confusing and difficult problem.
words.ex: Finding parking in the city is a daily conundrum.

words.def: Making someone very weak or unable to act normally.
words.ex: Malaria can be a debilitating disease.

words.def: Intended to teach, sometimes in a way that is too obvious.
words.ex: The novel was too didactic for my taste.

words.def: Including many different styles or sources.
words.ex: Her taste in music is eclectic.
words.origin: From French éclectique, from Ancient Greek ἐκλεκτικός (“selective”), from ἐκλέγω (“to pick, choose”), from ἐκ (“out, from”) + λέγω (“to choose, count”).

words.def: Extremely bad in a way that is easy to notice.
words.ex: It was an egregious mistake to ignore the warning.
words.origin: From Latin ēgregius, from e- (“out of”), + grex (“flock”), + English adjective suffix -ous, from Latin suffix -osus (“full of”); reflecting the positive connotations of "standing out from the flock".

words.def: Mysterious and difficult to understand.
words.ex: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile fascinates visitors.
words.origin: From Latin aenigmaticus and French énigmatique, from Ancient Greek αἰνιγματικός; equivalent to enigma + -tic.

words.def: Understood by only a small number of people with special knowledge.
words.ex: The lecture was full of esoteric terms.
words.origin: Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (“belonging to an inner circle”), from ἐσωτέρω (“further inside”), comparative of ἔσω (“within”), from ἐς, εἰς (“into”) (the term esoteric referred originally to the secret teachings of Greek philosophers, versus public or exoteric ones).

words.def: Very careful that everything is correct, clean or tidy.
words.ex: He is fastidious about keeping his desk clean.
words.origin: ”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness, arrogance, disgust”) + taedium (“disgust”). Cf. French fastidieux.

words.def: Done without a good reason; unnecessary.
words.ex: The film had too much gratuitous violence.
words.origin: From Latin grātuītus (“free”), from Latin grātia (“favor”), grātus (“showing favor”).

words.def: About to happen very soon.
words.ex: Dark clouds suggested a storm was imminent.
words.origin: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount).

words.def: Strange because it does not fit with what is around it.
words.ex: A modern sofa looked incongruous in the old palace.
words.origin: From Latin incongruus, from in- (“not”) + congruus (“congruent”), equivalent to in- + congruous.

words.def: Not harmful or offensive.
words.ex: It was an innocuous question, but she got upset.
words.origin: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

words.def: Refusing to change your opinion or behaviour.
words.ex: Both sides remained intransigent during the talks.
words.origin: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”), from trāns + agō.

words.def: Having little energy; feeling sleepy and slow.
words.ex: The heat made everyone lethargic.

words.def: Very many; too many to count.
words.ex: The night sky held a myriad of stars.

words.def: Wicked or criminal.
words.ex: The villain had a nefarious plan.
words.origin: From Latin nefārius (“execrable, abominable”), from nefās (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from ne- (“not”) + fās (“the dictates of religion, divine law”), which is related to Latin for (“to speak, to say”) and cognate to Ancient Greek φημί (“to say”).

words.def: Too eager to please or obey someone important.
words.ex: The obsequious waiter kept bowing to the minister.
words.origin: From Middle English obsequyous, from Latin obsequiōsus (“complaisant, obsequious”), from obsequium (“compliance”), from obsequor (“comply with, yield to”), from ob (“in the direction of, towards”) + sequor (“follow”) (cf.

words.def: So strong that it can almost be touched or felt.
words.ex: The excitement in the stadium was palpable.
words.origin: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō + -bilis.

words.def: Very unwilling to spend money.
words.ex: The parsimonious landlord refused to fix the roof.

words.def: Showing adult abilities at an unusually early age.
words.ex: The precocious girl was reading novels at six.
words.origin: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”).

words.def: Hopeful and romantic but not practical.
words.ex: His quixotic plan was to walk around the world.
words.origin: Derived from Spanish Quixote, the surname of Don Quixote, the title character in the novel by Miguel de Cervantes, + -ic.

words.def: Not willing to share thoughts or feelings.
words.ex: He was reticent about his childhood.
words.origin: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

words.def: Most important or noticeable.
words.ex: Summarise the salient points of the article.

words.def: Saying very little; not talkative.
words.ex: Her taciturn father rarely spoke at dinner.
words.origin: Back-formation from taciturnity, from Middle English taciturnite, from Latin taciturnitās; or alternatively from French taciturne, likely reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).

words.def: The fact of being everywhere.
words.ex: The ubiquity of smartphones has changed how we talk.
words.origin: From Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque.

words.def: Completely clear, leaving no doubt.
words.ex: The answer was an unequivocal yes.

words.def: Felt through the experiences of someone else.
words.ex: I get vicarious joy from my friend's travel photos.

words.def: Playful, unusual and a little silly.
words.ex: The children's book has whimsical drawings.

words.def: Sadly thinking about something you want or have lost.
words.ex: She gave a wistful look at the old house.
words.origin: Presumably from *whistful, from whist (“silent”) + -ful, based on older wistly. It is implausible that it derives from wishful, the required sound change being wishful → *wisful → wistful, which could not occur in Modern English, particularly not with wishful continuing in use.

words.def: The highest or most successful point.
words.ex: The empire reached its zenith in the 15th century.
